This ablation inventories all 30 estimator classes exported by Crabbymetrics and
measures how their fit time and memory use change over $n \in
\{10^3,10^4,10^5,10^6,10^7\}$ and $k \in \{5,10,20,50,100\}$. External
comparators follow a fixed preference order: scikit-learn, PyFixest, then a
canonical R implementation. A comparator is included in timing results only when
the common data-generating process preserves the estimator's semantics.

The full source inventory, exact GitHub references, dimension conventions, and
commands are in the [benchmark README](https://github.com/apoorvalal/crabbymetrics/blob/speedtest/benchmarks/scaling/README.md).

## Guard rails

Each cell runs in a fresh subprocess with single-threaded numerical kernels. The
driver rejects predicted over-cap allocations, watches aggregate descendant RSS,
enforces a wall timeout, and stops attempting larger samples after the first hard
failure for an estimator/implementation/dimension path. Thus a missing point is
an observed feasibility boundary, not an accidental omission.

```{python}
#| label: load-scaling-results
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

path = Path("data/estimator-scaling.csv")
results = pd.read_csv(path) if path.exists() else pd.DataFrame()
```

## Completion status

The committed run contains 1,150 cells across all 30 native estimators and 15
external implementation adapters. Of these, 731 completed, 198 were rejected by
the allocation preflight, 27 hit the 15-second timeout, five crossed the 1.83 GiB
hard RSS cap, and 189 larger cells were pruned after one of those hard failures.
No launched cell ended in an unclassified execution error.

```{python}
#| label: scaling-status
if results.empty:
    print("Run benchmarks/scaling/run_grid.py to populate the guarded grid.")
else:
    display(
        results.groupby(["implementation", "status"], dropna=False)
        .size()
        .rename("cells")
        .reset_index()
        .sort_values(["implementation", "status"])
    )
```

## Runtime frontier

```{python}
#| label: scaling-runtime
#| fig-cap: "Fit time by problem size; panels are estimator-specific because k has different semantics across families."
if not results.empty:
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    ok = results.loc[results.status.eq("ok")].copy()
    for estimator in ok.estimator.drop_duplicates():
        frame = ok.loc[ok.estimator.eq(estimator)]
        if frame.empty:
            continue
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
        for (implementation, k), group in frame.groupby(["implementation", "k"]):
            group = group.sort_values("n")
            ax.plot(group.n, group.fit_seconds, marker="o", label=f"{implementation}, k={k}")
        ax.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlabel="n", ylabel="fit seconds", title=estimator)
        ax.legend(fontsize=6, ncol=2)
        plt.show()
```

## Memory frontier

```{python}
#| label: scaling-memory
if not results.empty:
    frontier = (
        results.assign(peak_rss_gib=results.peak_rss_bytes / 2**30)
        .groupby(["estimator", "implementation", "status"], dropna=False)
        .agg(max_n=("n", "max"), max_peak_rss_gib=("peak_rss_gib", "max"))
        .reset_index()
    )
    display(frontier)
```

## Matched reference ratios

The table below uses only cells where both Crabbymetrics and the external
implementation completed. `reference / native > 1` means the Crabbymetrics fit
was faster; values below one mean the external fit was faster. Medians summarize
heterogeneous $(n,k)$ cells and should be read as a profiling signal, not a
single universal speed factor.

```{python}
#| label: matched-reference-ratios
if not results.empty:
    native = (
        results.loc[
            results.implementation.eq("crabbymetrics") & results.status.eq("ok"),
            ["estimator", "n", "k", "fit_seconds"],
        ]
        .rename(columns={"fit_seconds": "native_seconds"})
    )
    matched = (
        results.loc[
            results.implementation.ne("crabbymetrics") & results.status.eq("ok")
        ]
        .merge(native, on=["estimator", "n", "k"])
        .assign(reference_over_native=lambda frame: frame.fit_seconds / frame.native_seconds)
    )
    ratios = (
        matched.groupby(["estimator", "implementation"])
        .agg(
            matched_cells=("reference_over_native", "size"),
            median_reference_over_native=("reference_over_native", "median"),
        )
        .reset_index()
    )
    display(ratios)
```

## Interpretation

The grid is a systems benchmark, not an accuracy horse race. Fit-only timing is
reported; synthetic-data construction happens before the model call but remains
inside the child process and therefore contributes to the memory guard. Reference
rows test the same shapes and model family, but small differences in defaults,
parameterization, convergence criteria, and inference work remain. “Nearest”
references in the inventory are literature/code pointers only and never enter
the timing plots.

On this host, 26 of 30 native estimators completed at least one $n=10^6$ cell.
The native sample-size frontiers were $n=10^3$ for synthetic DID and augmented
balancing, $n=10^4$ for Cox PH and Andersen--Gill, and $n=10^6$ for the other 26
estimators. These maxima collapse across $k$ and therefore describe reach, not a
claim that every dimension completed at that sample size.
